en: The Scripture on Saving from Illness Spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle.
At that time, the Buddha was at the twin śāla trees...
Ānanda and immeasurable devas... [text fragment].

All the devas and humans gathered together. [The Buddha] returned to his seat and addressed Ānanda, saying: "My disciples and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... the realms of the various lands are peaceful, and the people are free from all calamities. The world is harmonious and compliant; they respectfully honor the Triple Gem. Those who would harm the Triple Gem—the Buddha remains at peace. Seeing these three persons, their bodies were covered in sores and filth, unfit for sight. Their speech faltered, their clothing was stained, and they bore heavy burdens upon their backs. Their gait was like that of one in great pain, seeking alms as their very livelihood."
The Buddha asked these three men, "Why have you come?
From which kingdoms are you the sons? They all remained silent.
The Buddha then questioned him earnestly;
though he was asked three times, he did not answer.
The Buddha immediately transformed him through skillful means.
The three replied,
"We are the sons of the Dark and Distressed;
why do you ask such a painful question?"
The Buddha asked these three men:
"From what does your illness arise?
By what means was it acquired?"
The three men replied,
"We do not know the cause of our affliction;
we were not even aware of the pain or itching, yet the sores have gradually increased in size."
"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causal origin of illness so that I may attain understanding.
The Buddha then addressed Ānanda and gathered his retinue;
eventually, the names of the seven Buddhas all arrived and sat together in assembly.
For this person's sake, I examined his past karma and then invoked the seven Buddhas:
first, Vipaśyin Buddha;
second, Śikhin Buddha.
The third was the Buddha Śiṣyaka;
the fourth was the Buddha Krakucchanda;
the fifth was the Buddha Kanakamuni.
The sixth was Kāśyapa Buddha;
the seventh was Śākyamuni Buddha.
These seven Buddhas all came together and sat in assembly.
The Buddha again asked the seven Buddhas,
"Whom did these three people give it to when they were ill?
The seven Buddhas each replied from the west.
"I have no one to give it to.
The Buddha then entered samādhi and meditative concentration,
observing the three illnesses with discernment to understand their fundamental causes.
The seven Buddhas addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, this illness does not arise from another;
it was brought upon oneself and has now manifested."
When Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Keeper of the Vajra, beholds an evil person,
he strikes them with his vajra, causing sores to break out on their face from the spittle [he spits upon them].
His beard and eyebrows fell off immediately;
this was caused by his offense against the Triple Gem.
The Buddha then asked:
“Vajrapāṇi, by what causes and conditions have these three persons fallen ill?
Vajrapāṇi replied,
“World-Honored One, my wish is to remain constantly at the Buddha’s side.”
In order to protect the Triple Gem,
so that evil persons may not cause harm to the Tathāgata and his virtuous mind may not sink,
I have seen these three people.
First, the offense of damaging images of the Tathāgata;
second, the offense of violating the True Dharma by plundering scriptures and images, thereby severing the holy teachings and causing the wholesome dharmas to sink and be blocked;
third, the offense of harming the noble Saṃgha by deceiving and injuring the great assembly.
This can cause the fourfold assembly of monks to eventually decline and perish.
Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Even if one were to offend other deities, their afflictions would not be like this."
One whose beard and eyebrows do not fall out,
or whose sores are itchy and suppurating, can be treated by those in the world;
however, one who has offended the Triple Gem cannot be cured by a teacher of worldly truth.
His face and body emitted a radiant light,
and fat issued forth from within his body.
Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Keeper, addressed the Buddha, saying:
I previously made a vow that when the World-Honored One attained the Way,
I would always remain by his side to protect the Triple Gem.
May the various māras, evil spirits, and wicked people not come to harass or afflict [us].
If there are wicked people who insult, humiliate, or steal from the Triple Gem,
I shall shatter their heads with my vajra-pestle.
"Just as the *ari* tree falls to the ground in seven pieces," Vajrapāṇi said to the Buddha,
"as for these three people..."
First, there are those who, from their parents up through seven generations of ancestors, have been bound by accumulated sins and thus receive this evil retribution;
or second, there are those who have committed minor offenses themselves without realizing it,
or who have intentionally committed transgressions but fail to repent in a timely manner.
Consequently, one's transgressions become increasingly thickened.
To treat this evil ailment, there is only one way:

to take refuge in the Buddhas with a heart of repentance, to confess before the Seven Buddhas, and to make a sincere vow with a vajra-like mind that the power of the Seven Buddhas may cause these heavy sins to be extinguished.
The Buddha told all sentient beings:
"If anyone takes property belonging to the Three Jewels,
regardless of whether it is hidden or manifest, one must repay many times over whatever enters their hands."
The seven Buddhas replied:
"If this is property belonging to the Buddha that has come into one's hands, it shall increase tenfold;
if it is not returned after ten years, [it becomes forfeit]."
Guhyapada will give rise to indignation and cause the one who takes it to suffer from a malignant disease.
If this scripture or image falls into their hands, its value shall increase sevenfold,
and it shall not be returned for seven years.
It can cause those who take it to suffer from malignant diseases;
if it is property belonging to the Sangha’s permanent endowment that has come into one's hands,
it shall be returned fivefold after five years.
Therefore, they give rise to deception and defiance, which can cause those who take [the medicine] to suffer from malignant diseases.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, the people of Jambudvīpa frequently give rise to lack of faith."
This means that those who commit offenses against the Triple Gem will incur grave illnesses and accumulate immeasurable sins.
Among the people of Jambudvīpa, there are those who kill their parents, harm the dharma rituals,
and even kill their paternal uncles, younger brothers, or those with whom they share astrological affinities.
If one can rectify the body, it can cause even malignant diseases to vanish.
If there is anyone who guarantees this as true and makes a vow before the Buddha on the six days of the fast, [their wish shall be fulfilled].
He sent messengers to deliver the responses:
sometimes descending as one of the Four Heavenly Kings,
and sometimes descending as a prince.
Sometimes a messenger descends;
sometimes one from the Heaven of the Thirty-three descends;
or sometimes a great seer descends.
Either descending from the realm of Akṣobhya,
or descending from the realm of the Vajrapāṇis;
on the day he is to descend.
The commentary states that humans, whether good or evil, ought to perform virtuous deeds and should not commit evil.
If there are those who steal or plunder objects belonging to the scriptures or images,
one should knowingly cause them to suffer from malignant diseases as a means of deterring such wickedness.
Some borrow gold, silver, copper, or iron;
others secretly take the property of the Triple Gem, as well as money, grain, silk, or cloth,
and even after a year has passed, they do not return them.
It can cause people to suffer malignant diseases;
or it may lead some to cast incantations and oaths against the Buddha’s image,
or to insult and mock the Buddha’s person.
Some burn or cook the sacred images and obscure or extinguish the words of the sutras;
others bring their wives to stay overnight within the monastic compound.
Or they may bring palace women into the Buddha’s stūpa to exchange secret pledges with them,
or they may engage in mutual lustful dalliance with the palace women.
Or there may be occurrences such as bodily afflictions or similar events that can cause a person to suffer from malignant diseases;
through such events, one shall fall ill after a long period of time.
Before even three years have passed,
there may be someone who secretly takes another's rice intended for a vegetarian feast;
if the host of the feast becomes aware of this and intentionally takes it, he can cause that person to suffer from a malignant disease.
If someone takes colored garments belonging to another and gives them to that person's wife,
both the recipient who knowingly accepts them and the giver shall incur guilt;
both parties will suffer from illness.
Or there may be those who secretly take miscellaneous vessels belonging to the Saṃgha or to nuns,
and knowing they have taken them, do not return them;
this can cause people to fall ill.
If someone engages in unchaste conduct with a statue or image of a cow or donkey,
it can cause that person to fall ill;
even though these are animals, such an act will cause illness for as long as three years.
Or if there is someone who brings a palace woman into a shrine of the Triple Gem to engage in impure acts,
it can cause people to fall ill.
Or if someone abducts a wife or a nun of pure conduct.
It can cause people to fall ill.
If someone places a scripture or an image inside a room but lacks a wooden box to contain it and keep it below, [this occurs].
If one sleeps with her,
it can cause people to fall ill;
within three years, their entire bodies will be afflicted by malignant diseases.
One should perform a severe repentance with a sense of urgency.
Offenses arise from the mind;
offenses are extinguished by the mind.
The mind is like heaven;
the mind is like hell.
To hold the palms upward is heaven.
To turn one's palms downward is hell.
If you wish to extinguish the heavy offenses within your body,
repent with a sincere heart and do not give rise to indolence or retreat.
The Buddha addressed the seven Buddhas, Vajrapāṇi, the great Bodhisattvas, and their retinues:
"How may these three types of sick persons be saved?
Then the Great Being Vajrapāṇi recounted the original causes and conditions.
This person is now to be pitied;
by skillful means and appropriate measures, one should rescue and deliver them so that they may be freed from the suffering of this illness.
The world proclaims the Tathāgata as being of great kindness and great compassion.
The seven Buddhas each addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, sentient beings are teeming and all possess Buddha-nature.
The illness of this person is easily removed and extinguished."
Now I shall ask you this myself:
Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada is my elder brother,
and Ānanda is my younger brother.
The number of my attendants is incalculable.
The seer Asita can ward off poisonous vapors;
the seer Ārāḍa can exorcise evil spirits.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three can descend with the water of the Dharma;
the Great Physician of the Snowy Mountains can bring down wondrous medicines;
and the nectar-like moisture of the Dharma can nourish that which is parched and withered.
King Ajātaśatru has committed grave offenses,
yet they can still be expiated;
his bodily sores shall be eliminated.
The Buddha, by means of skillful means, restored his body to its former state—neither digested nor extinguished.
This [perception] arose within the mind of the sick man.
The Buddha then used the contemplation of the mind’s reality or unreality to magically transform it into a great pit.
It was four thousand paces square and filled with glowing embers.
He questioned King Ajātaśatru.
"You can enter this great pit to extinguish your sins;
your wounds will be healed.
King Ajātaśatru said:
"If you can extinguish my sins,
I shall enter immediately.
King Ajātaśatru then burned incense before the Buddha and made this vow.
He leaps into the fire; having entered,
the water presses against his sides and transforms into a bathing pool,
whereby all his transgressions are extinguished.
It is like a person who dams a long-flowing river:
from above it flows as before, but once dammed at the bottom, it ceases.
Likewise, by taking refuge in all Buddhas and repenting of grave offenses, one is brought to cessation.
Thus, the extinction of lack of faith is difficult; the extinction of minor offenses is even more difficult.
The Buddha told the sick people:
"I shall instruct you."
One should simply, with a sincere mind, invite a virtuous Dharma Master to preside over the purification rites for one hundred days;
every day, pay homage to the names of the Seven Buddhas,
and every day, pay homage to Vajrapāṇi.
Every day he prostrated before Amitāyus Buddha.
Within a single day, he completed one scroll of the *Jiujing jing* (Scripture on Saving from Illness).
Within a hundred days, through the practice of the Way and repentance, he completed one hundred scrolls of the *Jidu jing* (Scripture on Deliverance).
"You may thus escape this karmic calamity and affliction;
do not harbor disbelief.
Thereupon, the sores increased in extent.
The Buddha’s words are not false;
the sutras are without error.
These are the words of the True Dharma.
"Most profound and most excellent!
Great disciples of the Buddhas,
this sutra is named 'The Sutra on Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings from Malignant Diseases.'"
*Jiujijing* (Sutra on Saving from Illness), one fascicle, intended to be circulated so that those in Jambudvīpa who are afflicted by disease may know and hear it.
